title: The Art of Abstention: Selective Prediction and Error Regularization for Natural Language Processing
research_question: How well do common confidence estimators support abstention in NLP classification, and can training-time error regularization improve the ordering of examples by confidence without materially reducing task accuracy?
methodology: The paper evaluates selective classification with LSTM, BERT-base, BERT-large, and ALBERT-base models on MRPC, QNLI, MNLI, and additional abstention experiments involving SST-5. It compares softmax response and Monte Carlo dropout as confidence estimators using risk-coverage AUC and reversed pair proportion in addition to conventional task metrics. The authors introduce pairwise error regularization that penalizes confidence orderings inconsistent with either current prediction error or a historical estimate of example difficulty, and they also test selective confidence in a two-model classifier cascade.

key_findings.finding: More capable Transformer classifiers generally achieved both better task accuracy and better selective-prediction quality than the LSTM baseline.

Softmax response was a strong confidence baseline and generally compared favorably with Monte Carlo dropout; the latter required roughly 20 stochastic repetitions before becoming competitive in the reported setting.

Pairwise error regularization improved confidence ranking while leaving task accuracy largely unchanged, with the best configurations reducing risk-coverage AUC by roughly 10% on average relative to unregularized training.
Neither current-error regularization nor history-based regularization consistently dominated the other across tasks and models.

In classifier cascades, confidence produced by an error-regularized first-stage model enabled a better accuracy-computation tradeoff than random routing and improved over the corresponding unregularized confidence strategy.

limitations: The empirical study focuses predominantly on classification benchmarks rather than generative question answering or multi-source generation.
GLUE development sets are used for evaluation because public test labels are unavailable, limiting strict separation between model development and final evaluation.
Monte Carlo dropout has significant inference cost because it requires many stochastic forward passes.
The pairwise regularizer is approximated with mini-batch pairs, and the history-based variant requires additional per-example state tracking during training.
The experiments do not identify a consistently superior definition of training error for regularization.
The method offers no finite-sample risk guarantee and no mechanism for continuous recalibration under domain or temporal drift.
The paper does not address evidence completeness, partially supported compound claims, or longitudinal new, resolved, and superseded work-item states.
raw_claims: Selective prediction combines an ordinary classifier with a confidence score used to decide whether to abstain.
The paper evaluates LSTM and several Transformer models on standard NLP classification datasets.
Risk-coverage AUC and reversed pair proportion are used to measure selective behavior.
The proposed regularizer penalizes pairs whose confidence ordering conflicts with their relative prediction errors.
One regularizer uses current errors while another uses historical errors accumulated during training.
Error regularization usually improves selective metrics without materially changing classification accuracy.
Monte Carlo dropout requires repeated stochastic inference and is computationally more expensive than a single softmax-response evaluation.
The classifier-cascade experiment routes low-confidence examples from a cheaper model to a stronger model.
The authors provide public source code for the experiments.
